from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
def fit_predict(train, inputs, seed):
    model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),Ridge(alpha=10.0))
    model.fit(train['X'],train['y'])
    return model.predict(inputs['X']).tolist()

steps.hypothesis: Question: does the strong development result of the raw-target HistGradientBoosting reference (idea-baseline-2, action d81da712..., dev RMSE 59.99 vs Ridge 182.95 vs median 268.48) rest on relationships that transfer to a later period, or partly on a non-extrapolable level feature? Trees cannot extrapolate elapsed_day beyond the training range, and the raw-count target forces the model to learn hour-by-level interactions additively even though rental growth from 2011 to 2012 is plausibly multiplicative (hourly pattern scaled by a rising volume). Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) log1p target and/or dropping elapsed_day transfer better on a chronological internal holdout (last 61 training dates, future-period transfer rather than interpolation) and reduce negative bias on high-volume 2012 hours; (B) raw target wins because RMSE is dominated by peak hours and log fitting under-weights them, and elapsed_day helps by pinning the latest level via its last leaf. The program runs all 6 combinations, selects by internal holdout RMSE, refits on the full train set, and reports internal RMSE/MAE/bias, the selected branch, a 2012/2011 same-month level-ratio diagnostic, and any fallback use. Prior evidence changed my view only in that the Ridge->HGB gap shows nonlinear hour/weather structure is essential, so I keep the HGB core and vary only target scale and the trend feature. Note: early_stopping is set to False explicitly (the reference used sklearn's auto early stopping since train exceeds 10000 rows), so this is a joint change, not a one-factor attribution to the transform alone. Exploratory and unverified until executed.

Question: does the 2011->2012 level shift transfer as a continuing multiplicative growth trend, a plateau, or is it already absorbed by the baseline HGB via the yr feature? Evidence: idea-59da36 (action 2d119fec...) measured internal pseudo-future holdout (cut elapsed_day 425, 61 days) with systematic negative bias for every variant (-54 to -97 rides/hour) and year_level_by_month ratios of 1.84-2.53x, i.e. trees trained mostly on 2011 underpredict later periods and elapsed_day makes it worse (raw|all rmse 115.5 vs raw|no_elapsed_day 95.2). Yet its internally selected sqrt|no_elapsed_day scored dev RMSE 63.04, worse than the plain baseline HGB with all features (idea-baseline-2, 59.99), so a single far-extrapolative holdout misranked candidates; this changed my view: level must be modeled explicitly, and internal selection should use two forward-chained 30-day folds closer to the real train/dev gap and must include the baseline itself as a candidate. Method: HGB on log1p(cnt) using shape features (all except elapsed_day and yr) plus an additive daily log-level offset estimated from cross-fitted (5 contiguous date blocks) out-of-block daily mean residuals; offset for future days is 'none', 'const60' (mean of last 60 training days), 'trend_all' (linear in elapsed_day over all training days) or 'trend180' (linear over last 180 days). Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) trend variants win internally and reduce dev RMSE below 59.99 with pred_mean well above train_mean -> growth continues and is transferable; (B) const60 wins -> level shift transfers as a plateau, trend extrapolation overshoots (positive bias); (C) baseline_all_raw wins or level variants show larger dev RMSE -> the yr indicator already captures the transferable level and residual-level modeling adds noise. Findings report all fold metrics, fitted slopes/constants, the actually selected branch after refitting and any fallback. Unverified exploratory reasoning; a joint change (log target + feature drop + offset), so one-factor attribution is not claimed.

steps.hypothesis: Question: recorded rentals grew strongly from 2011 to early 2012 (train mean 154 vs last-60-day mean 232 in idea-f87923 findings). Which representation of that level shift transfers into May-June 2012? Prior evidence: idea-baseline-2 (squared-error HGB, all features incl. elapsed_day and yr, dev RMSE 59.99, group MAE 40.95) is the best valid measurement; idea-f87923's detached additive log1p level offset (const60=+0.55, i.e. ~1.74x on a shape model trained without yr/elapsed_day) selected by a 2-fold internal comparison overshot badly on dev (pred_mean 334, RMSE 93.3), and its two internal folds disagreed on the sign of the raw baseline's bias (-45 vs +8). This changed my view: bolting a separately estimated level onto a shape model plus small-fold selection is fragile; the level should be learned jointly with the covariates, and internal folds should serve as diagnostics, not as the selector. Proposal: hold every baseline-2 hyperparameter fixed (max_iter=250, lr=0.08, max_leaf_nodes=31, l2=1, random_state=1729, default early_stopping='auto', which with >10000 rows is likely active; n_iter_ is reported) and change only loss='poisson', submitting that model with all features. Contrasting expectations: (A) if rentals scale multiplicatively (hour/weather shape x growth level), the Poisson link lets the same trees represent the yr/elapsed_day effect as a ratio and dev RMSE falls below 59.99 with reduced |bias| on the recorded holdouts; (B) if dev error is dominated by high-count hourly noise, Poisson deviance down-weights large-count errors and dev RMSE is equal or worse (an informative negative for the multiplicative-transfer view). Diagnostics only (no selection): three chronological 30-day holdouts (cuts at last-90/-60/-30 train days) comparing squared_all, poisson_all and poisson without elapsed_day, reporting RMSE/MAE/bias/pred_mean per fold, plus the Jan-Apr 2012/2011 mean ratio to expose the raw growth factor. Any fit failure falls back to squared_error and is reported in findings. One city and one 61-day period cannot establish general benefit.

findings.design: poisson HGB (parent hparams, all features) fitted on y/L(day), L=exp(damp*b*(day-last_fit_day)); b = median log year-over-year ratio of daily mean hourly cnt / 365, estimated from the fitting window only; damp selected by mean RMSE over 3 chronological folds with 61-day horizon

steps.hypothesis: Question: the development leader idea-a0bc19 (Poisson HGB, all features, loss 54.01, group MAE 35.89) recorded jan_apr_level_ratio_2012_over_2011 = 2.10 and a fold at cut_426 with bias -49 (holdout mean 222 vs pred mean 173), while trees cannot extrapolate elapsed_day beyond day 485 (eval range 486-546). Does an explicit multiplicative growth offset L(day)=exp(b*(day-last_train_day)), with b estimated only from year-over-year matched daily mean-hourly ratios in the fitting window, transfer into the later period? Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) growth continues -> full offset (damp 1.0) removes the negative bias seen at later cuts, internal 61-day-horizon folds and development RMSE fall below 54; (B) growth saturated or startup-inflated (Jan-Apr 2011 was ramp-up) -> full offset overshoots with positive bias, damp 0.5 or 0.0 wins internally and any dev gain is small or negative; (C) the internal selection is unstable across the three folds, indicating the growth signal is too noisy for a 61-day horizon. Evidence changed my view: the parent's fold bias pattern (-49 at cut_426 but +5 at cut_456) means growth is not uniform, so the program selects a damping factor in {0, 0.5, 1} by mean RMSE over three chronological folds with a 61-day horizon matching development, and reports the selected branch, the estimated b, implied annual factor and implied factor at eval mid-point. This is a joint change (target normalization + internal selection) relative to the parent; same HGB hyperparameters and features are held fixed. Unverified exploratory rationale; a dev gain would need confirmation-period transfer.

findings.design: poisson HGB (idea-a0bc19 hparams, all features) with exponential recency sample weights w=0.5**((last_fit_day-day)/half_life), normalized to mean 1; half-life selected by mean RMSE over 3 chronological folds with 61-day horizon, ties toward hl_none; only sample weights vary

steps.hypothesis: Question: do older (2011 start-up regime) hourly records help or hurt transfer to a later period when the model is otherwise fixed? Evidence so far: the development leader idea-a0bc19 (plain Poisson HGB, all features, uniform weights) scored loss 54.01 / group MAE 35.89 with pred_mean 264.3 vs train_last60_mean 232.5; its child idea-2a518e imposed an explicit exponential YoY growth factor (selected damp 1.0, implied factor 1.068 at eval mid, pred_mean 296.5) and got worse (65.18 / 41.55), so explicit level extrapolation overshot even though its internal folds preferred it. Both programs' internal spring fold (cut ~425) showed about -100 bias for every variant, i.e. a level jump no candidate captured, which makes the internal fold mean a weak selector. This changed my view: instead of extrapolating a trend, test whether de-emphasizing the early-2011 regime (recency sample weights with half-life in {none,365,180,90} days, weights normalized to mean 1, identical hparams and features to idea-a0bc19) lets the tree model learn a level/profile closer to the recent regime without extrapolation. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if 2011 relationships transfer well, hl_none wins internally and dev loss stays ~54 -- an informative negative result that the full history is worth keeping; (B) if the ramp-up regime distorts learned levels, hl_180 or hl_90 wins internally and dev loss drops below 54 with pred_mean modestly above 264; (C) a possible regression: weighting shrinks effective sample size (reported per fold) and could raise variance, giving worse dev RMSE even if internal folds favor it, as happened with idea-2a518e. Selection is by mean RMSE over 3 chronological 61-day-horizon folds with ties resolved toward uniform weights; the program reports the selected half-life, per-fold results, effective sample sizes and any fallback. Single-factor design: only sample weights vary.

findings.design: HGB variants with idea-a0bc19 hparams (max_iter=250,lr=0.08,leaves=31,l2=1,seed=1729): poisson all features, poisson without mnth/season, squared_error all features, and their simple averages; branch selected by mean RMSE over 3 chronological folds with 61-day horizon, ties toward poisson_all (identical to a0bc19 submission)

steps.hypothesis: Question: does the development leader (idea-a0bc19, Poisson HGB all features, dev RMSE 54.009) leave recoverable error from (a) year-by-month interactions that cannot transfer to unseen (yr=1, mnth) combinations and (b) single-model variance, such that averaging comparable HGB variants or dropping mnth/season improves later-period transfer? Recorded evidence: a0bc19 internal folds gave poisson_all 60.80 vs squared_all 60.96 mean RMSE with opposite-signed biases in cut_396/cut_456, suggesting partially complementary errors; poisson_no_elapsed was worse (63.53), so elapsed_day is kept. idea-cf138a showed recency weighting did not help (hl_none selected in all 3 folds, identical submission to a0bc19, dev RMSE 54.009), which moved my view away from time-weighting and toward representation/ensemble questions. The cut_425 fold (train through mid-March 2012, holdout Mar-Apr 2012) had bias -104 for every candidate, indicating the spring level shift is the dominant untransferred component and is unlikely to be fixed by these variants; this test is therefore bounded. Contrasting expected outcomes: (1) avg_poisson_all_squared or avg_all_three wins internal folds by 1-3% mean RMSE and submits a slightly lower dev RMSE (<54.0); (2) poisson_no_month_season wins if month effects are mostly weather proxies whose year-interaction fails to transfer; (3) poisson_all wins all folds, in which case the program submits exactly the a0bc19 predictor (ties favor it) and the informative result is that feature-subset/loss averaging does not help, leaving a0bc19 as the fixed selection. Only sample-independent model variants of the same hyperparameters vary; the selection is by mean RMSE over 3 chronological 61-day folds as in cf138a. Fallbacks are reported explicitly. Unverified: whether development gains would transfer to Jul-Dec 2012 where yr=1 and mnth>=7 are jointly unseen.

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
def fit_predict(train, inputs, seed):
    model=make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),Ridge(alpha=10.0))
    model.fit(train['X'],train['y'])
    return model.predict(inputs['X']).tolist()

findings.note: selection uses only training dates; no evaluation covariates used beyond prediction

steps.hypothesis: Question: does the 2011->2012 growth in recorded rentals transfer into May-June 2012 as a multiplicative factor on the hour/weather/calendar profile, and does an additive raw-count HGB fail to carry it? Evidence: HGB (idea-baseline-2, dev RMSE 59.99, group MAE 40.95) beats standardized Ridge (182.95) and median (268.48) by a large margin, showing nonlinear hr x workingday x weather structure dominates; but raw-count HGB fits additive leaf values and cannot exceed levels seen in training, and May-June with yr=1 is an unseen mnth x yr cell. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if growth is a roughly stable multiplicative factor, HGB on log1p(cnt) (branch 'log') or log-detrended HGB with linear log-trend extrapolation ('log_trend', elapsed_day and yr dropped from the trees) wins the internal forward folds (last two 61-day blocks of train, fit on strictly earlier dates) and lowers dev RMSE below 59.99 without worsening equal-date MAE; (B) if growth is not stable or trend extrapolation overshoots summer 2012, 'raw' wins or log_trend regresses, which would be an informative negative about trend transfer; (C) a mismatch between the internally selected branch and the dev outcome would indicate that forward validation on Jan-Apr 2012 does not proxy the May-June transfer. The program reports the selected branch, fold RMSEs, fitted annual growth factor, any exception-based fallback to 'raw', and nonfinite replacements, so the selection can be audited. Joint change (target transform + selection) is exploratory; single-factor attribution is available only via the reported per-branch fold scores. Unverified until executed.

findings.note: branch selection uses only training dates (two forward 61-day holdouts); evaluation covariates used only for final prediction; baseline HGB hyperparameters fixed

steps.hypothesis: Question: does the hourly-rental structure transfer to a later period better as an additive (squared_error) or multiplicative (Poisson log-link, or log1p target) relationship within the same HistGradientBoosting learner? Prior evidence: idea-baseline-2 (HGB, all features, squared error) reached development RMSE 59.99 / equal-date MAE 40.95, while idea-ea0e19 dropped elapsed_day/yr and imposed a parametric log-trend, ending at 122.13 — its own forward folds showed the plain log branch was worst in the most recent fold (140.6 vs 116.6 raw), which revised my view: removing the tree's direct access to yr/elapsed_day level information hurt, and a pure log target may shrink peak-hour predictions that dominate RMSE. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) Poisson loss keeps the multiplicative hour x working-day x weather scaling and matches or beats squared error on forward RMSE (<= ~58 on development) and improves equal-date MAE; (B) squared error remains best on RMSE because RMSE is dominated by peak counts and Poisson under-weights large residuals; (C) log1p target wins on equal-date MAE but loses on RMSE, replicating the ea0e19 pattern. The program selects the branch by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day holdouts using only training dates, reports per-branch fold RMSE and per-date MAE, refits the selected branch on all training rows, and reports any fallback. Only baseline HGB hyperparameters are held fixed, so a single factor (objective/target transform) is varied. Unverified exploratory expectation; one city/two years cannot establish general benefit.

findings.note: growth rate b fitted on log daily totals of training dates only (trend + 2 harmonics); target deflated by exp(b*(day-last_train_day)) and predictions re-inflated; branch selection by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day training holdouts; HGB hyperparameters fixed at baseline; evaluation covariates used only for final prediction

steps.hypothesis: Question: the parent (idea-ae78bf, action 8305d9ba...) kept the baseline HGB (squared branch selected; dev RMSE 59.976 vs baseline 59.993, effectively unchanged) and showed forward-holdout RMSE far worse than development (fold1 days 424-485: 116.6; fold2: 74.9). Tree models predict a flat level beyond the training day range, so a continuing 2011->2012 growth trend cannot be extrapolated by elapsed_day/yr splits; the log1p and poisson branches, which encode multiplicative structure, were nevertheless worse on those forward folds, so a pure loss change is not the fix. This program tests a separable trend: fit log daily totals on training dates only as a + b*day + two day-of-year harmonics, deflate the target by exp(b*(day-last_train_day)), fit the same fixed-hyperparameter squared-error HGB on the deflated target, and re-inflate predictions with the extrapolated factor. Two deflated variants (drop yr/elapsed_day so the trend must live in the deflator; keep all features) are compared with the unchanged squared branch using the parent's two forward 61-day holdouts, with b re-estimated inside each fold. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if the level shift is a persistent exponential trend, deflated branches cut forward-fold RMSE materially (fold1 well below 116) and the program selects a deflated branch, giving dev RMSE below 59.98; (B) if growth has saturated or is seasonal confounding, the deflator over-predicts, deflated branches lose on forward folds, the program keeps 'squared' and the dev result matches the parent, an informative negative result about trend transfer. Findings expose the estimated daily growth rate and implied annual factor per fold and for the final refit, so the selected branch and its trend assumption are visible. Note the branch selection is by forward-holdout RMSE only; a 5% dev gain from this single 61-day period would still not establish transfer to July-December. Unverified until executed.

findings.note: lag features are training-label counts at elapsed_day-364 same hr (point) or mean of lag 357/364/371 same hr plus mean daily total over lag week (smooth); NaN when unavailable; tables built only from the fold/final training labels; branch selection by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day training holdouts; fold 2 training rows have no lag so its lag branches cannot learn lag relations; HGB hyperparameters fixed at baseline; evaluation covariates used only for final prediction

steps.hypothesis: Question: does the level relationship between a 2012 hour and the same hour one year (52 weeks, weekday-aligned) earlier transfer into the later period better than (a) letting trees infer level from yr/elapsed_day alone or (b) a global exponential trend? Prior evidence changed my view: idea-816bb1 fitted a global log-linear trend (annual factor 2.16 on train-only daily totals) and deflated/re-inflated targets; it degraded development RMSE to 81.03 vs 59.98 for the fixed-HGB leader idea-ae78bf (which itself matched baseline-2 at 59.99, so target-transform branches added nothing). This suggests a global multiplicative growth extrapolation overshoots, while trees using yr already carry most of the transferable level. Instead of extrapolating a trend, this program supplies a local anchor: for each row, the training-label rental count at elapsed_day-364 with the same hr ('lag_point'), and a smoothed version averaging the same hour at lag 357/364/371 plus the mean daily total over the week around lag 364 ('lag_smooth'), both alongside the original covariates; missing values (all 2011 rows) are left NaN for HGB. Branches base/lag_point/lag_smooth use identical fixed baseline HGB hyperparameters and are selected by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day training holdouts exactly as in idea-ae78bf, so the only changed factor per branch is the feature set. Contrasting expectations: if the previous-year hourly relationship transfers, lag_smooth should beat base in fold 1 (holdout Mar-Apr 2012, the only fold where training rows carry lags) and development RMSE should fall below ~57 (>=5% relative gain) without equal-date MAE worsening; if the lag columns act mainly as a yr proxy confounded with missingness, or previous-year weather noise dominates, the gain will be nil (~60) or negative, which would be an informative negative about year-over-year hourly transfer. Fold 2 (holdout Jan-Feb 2012) cannot learn lag relationships because all its training rows are 2011; this is reported rather than hidden. The program also reports train-only year-over-year monthly daily-total ratios for Jan-Apr 2012 vs 2011 to check the 2.16 annual factor assumed by idea-816bb1. Program-authored findings are diagnostics on training data only, not evaluation-label metrics.

findings.note: yoy_scaled: HGB (baseline hyperparameters, squared error) fit on cnt divided by a +/-14-day smoothed mean hourly count per training date; evaluation-date level = smoothed level at elapsed_day-364 times geometric-mean YoY ratio over trailing 56 training days (clipped to [0.5,4]); persistence of last training level when no analog; blend = 0.5*(base+yoy_scaled); selection by mean forward RMSE over training folds with analog coverage >= 50 percent (all folds if none); only evaluation elapsed_day is used for analog lookup; no evaluation labels anywhere

steps.hypothesis: Question: is the forward-transfer error of the HGB reference dominated by the aggregate rental LEVEL (growth between periods) rather than by the within-day/weather shape? Evidence that changed my view: idea-325a52 (valid, dev loss 59.976, base branch selected) reported forward fold 1 RMSE 116.6 for base HGB (train through day 424, holdout Mar-Apr 2012) versus 59.98 on development, and a 2012-vs-2011 daily-total ratio of 2.14 overall (Jan 2.51, Feb 2.03, Mar 2.55, Apr 1.78). Lag COUNTS as extra covariates (lag_point/lag_smooth) did not help because a tree cannot learn a lag relation for rows lacking lag support and cannot extrapolate level beyond seen yr/elapsed_day values. idea-ae78bf showed log1p/poisson losses did not beat squared error, so this program keeps squared-error HGB with baseline hyperparameters and instead changes the REPRESENTATION: target z = cnt / S(date), where S is a centered +/-14-day smoothed mean hourly count from training labels only; HGB fits z on features without yr/elapsed_day; the evaluation-date level is extrapolated as S(date-364)*r with r the geometric-mean YoY ratio of smoothed levels over the trailing 56 training days (clipped to [0.5,4] and reported), falling back to the last training level (persistence) when no analog exists, with the persistence fraction reported. Branches: base (reference HGB), yoy_scaled, blend (0.5/0.5). Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if level shift is the main transferable error, yoy_scaled beats base clearly on fold 1 (where base was 116.6) and on development, and blend or yoy_scaled is selected with dev RMSE below 59.98; (B) if 2012 growth decelerates (April ratio 1.78 vs ~2.1 earlier) the trailing ratio over-scales, yoy_scaled is worse than base and base is re-selected, giving an informative negative result (dev loss expected to reproduce ~59.98). Pre-stated selection rule: branch with lowest mean forward RMSE over the training folds where the analog level had >=50% coverage (fold 2 has no 364-day analog in training, as 325a52 noted, so it is excluded from selection when unsupported); selection over all folds is also reported. Confirmation caveat: after refit on train+dev the level for Jul-Dec 2012 will be Jul-Dec 2011 levels times a May-Jun 2012 ratio, so any further deceleration of growth would hurt; equal-date MAE of the selected branch is reported per fold to watch the milestone constraint. Transductive use of evaluation covariates: only elapsed_day of evaluation rows is used to look up analog training levels; no evaluation labels exist in any lookup.

findings.note: same two forward 61-day training holdouts as idea-ae78bf; candidates: baseline HGB, slower/more regularized HGB, and date-bootstrap bags (6 bags, whole-date resampling via sample_weight multiplicity) of each; squared error throughout; selection by mean forward RMSE, ties by branch order; evaluation covariates used only for final prediction; no evaluation labels

steps.hypothesis: Question: is the remaining development error of the HGB leader dominated by estimator variance/capacity (fixable by bagging or a slower, more regularized boosting schedule) or by period-level shift (not fixable without level extrapolation)? Contrasting expectations: (A) variance/capacity dominates -> a date-bootstrap bag of 6 HGBs or a 600-iteration lr=0.04 min_samples_leaf=40 HGB lowers development RMSE by roughly 1-4% versus 59.98; (B) transfer/level shift dominates -> all branches stay within about 1% of the leader and forward-fold RMSE remains far above development RMSE, confirming that interpolation-style variance reduction does not address the transfer gap. How prior evidence changed my view: idea-ae78bf showed loss/target transforms are not the lever (59.976 vs baseline HGB 59.993, essentially identical), and idea-fa3d93 showed that aggressive YoY level scaling selected by forward folds (yoy_ratio 2.09, blend chosen, forward fold RMSE 71 vs base 117) badly hurt development RMSE (99.8 vs 60), so within-training forward folds overstate the level gap that the final model (which sees Jan-Apr 2012) actually faces. I therefore stop pursuing level extrapolation and run the conservative check; bootstrap by whole dates respects within-date dependence. Selection uses the same two 61-day forward holdouts as idea-ae78bf so the selection protocol is held fixed; only the candidate set changes. Unverified exploratory rationale; if worse than the leader the default lowest-development-RMSE selection still applies.

scope: One pair per model on one public bicycle-rental dataset with chronological split and observed weather. Six final months do not establish operational forecast validity, causal growth/weather mechanisms, literature novelty, or stable general research benefit. B pairs recent/last-valid/leader source with findings; A shows latest findings and leader source. Both allow repairs and identical syntax. Exact edits preserve text, not necessarily one scientific factor.
